---
title: "Interpolation"
subtitle: "ConvolutionInterpolations.jl against Interpolations.jl, BSplineKit.jl and Dierckx.jl"
engine: julia
---

Interpolation of a difficult function from uniformly spaced samples: the convolution kernels
against the cubic B-spline of Interpolations.jl, the B-spline interpolants of BSplineKit.jl at
cubic and high order, and the quintic FITPACK spline of Dierckx.jl. First the accuracy as the
grid is refined, then the time to construct an interpolant and the time to evaluate it, in one
and two dimensions, and finally the two together: the time each method needs to reach a given
accuracy.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Packages and the methods"
using ConvolutionInterpolations
import Interpolations                # qualified: exports `interpolate`, as BSplineKit does
import BSplineKit
import Dierckx
using Chairmarks, Printf, Random, CairoMakie

# each method maps (x, y) on a uniform grid to a callable interpolant
methods_1d = [
    "Interpolations.jl cubic" => (x, y) -> Interpolations.scale(
        Interpolations.interpolate(y, Interpolations.BSpline(Interpolations.Cubic(Interpolations.Line(Interpolations.OnGrid())))), x),
    "BSplineKit k=4"          => (x, y) -> BSplineKit.interpolate(x, y, BSplineKit.BSplineOrder(4)),
    "BSplineKit k=8"          => (x, y) -> BSplineKit.interpolate(x, y, BSplineKit.BSplineOrder(8)),
    "Dierckx k=5"             => (x, y) -> Dierckx.Spline1D(collect(x), collect(y); k = 5),
    "ConvInterp :a4"          => (x, y) -> convolution_interpolation(x, y; kernel = :a4),
    "ConvInterp :b5"          => (x, y) -> convolution_interpolation(x, y; kernel = :b5),
    "ConvInterp :b7"          => (x, y) -> convolution_interpolation(x, y; kernel = :b7),
]

runge(x) = 1 / (1 + 25x^2)                                # Runge's function
xr = range(-1, 1, length = 2001);                         # fine points for measuring the error
```

## Convergence

The largest error against Runge's function on the fine points, as the number of samples
doubles:

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "The convergence study"
ns = [21, 41, 81, 161, 321, 641, 1281]
hs = 2 ./ (ns .- 1)
errs = Dict(name => Float64[] for (name, _) in methods_1d)
for n in ns
    x = range(-1, 1, length = n)
    y = runge.(x)
    for (name, m) in methods_1d
        itp = m(x, y)
        push!(errs[name], maximum(abs.(itp.(xr) .- runge.(xr))))
    end
end

fig = Figure(size = (800, 420))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xreversed = true,
                     xlabel = "spacing h", ylabel = "largest error")
for (name, _) in methods_1d
    scatterlines!(ax, hs, max.(errs[name], 1e-17); markersize = 8, label = name)
end
lines!(ax, hs, errs["ConvInterp :b7"][end] .* (hs ./ hs[end]) .^ 7; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, label = "slope 7")
Legend(fig[1, 2], ax)
fig
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
# the observed order between the two finest grids still clear of rounding
println("| | observed order | error at the finest grid |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|")
for (name, _) in methods_1d
    e = errs[name]
    i = findlast(v -> v > 1e-13, e); i = max(i, 2)
    @printf("| %s | %.2f | %.1e |\n", name, log(e[i-1] / e[i]) / log(hs[i-1] / hs[i]), e[end])
end
```

The cubic methods — Interpolations.jl, BSplineKit at order 4, and `:a4` — converge at 4th
order; Dierckx's quintic at 6th, as does `:b5`; BSplineKit at order 8 and `:b7` at 7th. The
difference between the last two is not the order but what it costs, which the timings show.

## Setup and query

Construction time for a grid of a thousand samples, and evaluation time per point at a million
random points, each interpolant built once and evaluated in one broadcast:

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "The 1D timings"
rng = MersenneTwister(1)
n1 = 1000
x1 = range(-1, 1, length = n1)
y1 = runge.(x1)
p1 = rand(rng, 1_000_000) .* 1.98 .- 0.99                  # a million random points inside the grid

rows_1d = map(methods_1d) do (name, m)
    t_setup = (@b $m($x1, $y1)).time
    itp = m(x1, y1)
    t_query = (@b $itp.($p1)).time / length(p1)
    (name = name, t_setup = t_setup, t_query = t_query)
end;
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
fmt(t) = t < 1e-6 ? @sprintf("%.0f ns", 1e9 * t) :
         t < 1e-3 ? @sprintf("%.1f μs", 1e6 * t) :
         t < 1    ? @sprintf("%.2f ms", 1e3 * t) : @sprintf("%.2f s", t)
println("| | setup, 1000 samples | query, per point |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|")
for r in rows_1d
    println("| ", r.name, " | ", fmt(r.t_setup), " | ", fmt(r.t_query), " |")
end
```

In two dimensions, a 200 × 200 grid and two hundred thousand random points. Interpolations.jl
and Dierckx have tensor-product interpolants; BSplineKit's are one-dimensional, so it is not
in this table:

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "The 2D timings"
n2 = 200
x2 = range(-1, 1, length = n2)
y2 = range(-1, 1, length = n2)
z2 = [runge(xi) * runge(yi) for xi in x2, yi in y2]
px = rand(rng, 200_000) .* 1.98 .- 0.99
py = rand(rng, 200_000) .* 1.98 .- 0.99

methods_2d = [
    "Interpolations.jl cubic" => () -> Interpolations.scale(
        Interpolations.interpolate(z2, Interpolations.BSpline(Interpolations.Cubic(Interpolations.Line(Interpolations.OnGrid())))), x2, y2),
    "Dierckx k=5"             => () -> Dierckx.Spline2D(collect(x2), collect(y2), z2; kx = 5, ky = 5),
    "ConvInterp :a4"          => () -> convolution_interpolation((x2, y2), z2; kernel = :a4),
    "ConvInterp :b5"          => () -> convolution_interpolation((x2, y2), z2; kernel = :b5),
    "ConvInterp :b7"          => () -> convolution_interpolation((x2, y2), z2; kernel = :b7),
]

rows_2d = map(methods_2d) do (name, m)
    t_setup = (@b $m()).time
    itp = m()
    t_query = if itp isa Dierckx.Spline2D
        (@b Dierckx.evaluate($itp, $px, $py)).time / length(px)   # Dierckx evaluates point lists through `evaluate`
    else
        (@b $itp.($px, $py)).time / length(px)
    end
    (name = name, t_setup = t_setup, t_query = t_query)
end;
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
println("| | setup, 200 × 200 samples | query, per point |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|")
for r in rows_2d
    println("| ", r.name, " | ", fmt(r.t_setup), " | ", fmt(r.t_query), " |")
end
```

The convolution interpolants compute nothing at construction beyond the boundary values, and
evaluate in a fixed number of operations per point — the stencil's — whatever the grid size,
with the cell located by one division per axis. A B-spline interpolant solves a banded system
at construction and searches for the cell at evaluation; a FITPACK spline does both in Fortran.
The tables show where each trade lands.

## Time to accuracy

When the samples are given, the convergence plot is the measure: the error at that grid is what
you get. When the sampling is yours to choose — a table you generate, output you resample — the
question becomes which method reaches a given accuracy in the least time, and a finer grid is
allowed if it pays. The work–precision diagram puts the two together: for each method and each
grid of the convergence study, the time to construct the interpolant and evaluate it at a
hundred thousand points, against the error on that grid. A curve further left reaches the same
accuracy in less time.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "The work–precision study"
pw = rand(rng, 100_000) .* 1.98 .- 0.99                   # the evaluation workload
times = Dict(name => Float64[] for (name, _) in methods_1d)
for n in ns
    x = range(-1, 1, length = n)
    y = runge.(x)
    for (name, m) in methods_1d
        push!(times[name], (@b begin itp = $m($x, $y); itp.($pw) end).time)
    end
end

fig = Figure(size = (800, 420))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10,
          xlabel = "time to construct and evaluate at 10⁵ points [s]", ylabel = "largest error")
for (name, _) in methods_1d
    scatterlines!(ax, times[name], max.(errs[name], 1e-17); markersize = 8, label = name)
end
Legend(fig[1, 2], ax)
fig
```

Each curve descends as its grid refines, and the curves are nearly vertical: at a hundred
thousand evaluations the time is the evaluation, for every method, and a finer grid costs
almost nothing. A method's position left to right is therefore its cost per point, and the
depth of its curve is how far its order takes it. The spline of order 8 needs fewer samples
than `:b7` for a given error and reaches rounding later; the cubic B-spline and `:b5` cost the
same per point, and `:b5` goes five decades deeper. The kernels are first to any accuracy down
to rounding, which is the trade they were designed for.
